claim: IgG4 is the least potent human IgG subclass for the FcγR-mediated antibody effector function.
source: IgG4 is the least potent human IgG subclass for the FcγR-mediated antibody effector function.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript (Lighaam and Rispens, 2016; Vidarsson et al., 2014).

claim: IgG4 is the dominant IgG subclass of pathogenic autoantibodies in IgG4-mediated diseases.
source: IgG4 is also the dominant IgG subclass of pathogenic autoantibodies in IgG4-mediated diseases.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by patient data analysis showing IgG4 dominance in PF patients (Figure 4A) and references to literature (Huijbers et al., 2018; Koneczny, 2018).

claim: IgG4 and its weak Fc-FcγR interaction have an ameliorative role in the pathogenicity of anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies isolated from TTP patients.
source: While IgG4 and its weak Fc-FcγR interaction have an ameliorative role in the pathogenicity of anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies isolated from thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) patients
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing faster recovery of ADAMTS13 activity in mice treated with IgG4 vs IgG1 anti-ADAMTS13 antibodies (Figure 1B, C, D, E).

claim: IgG4 and its weak Fc-FcγR interaction have an exacerbating effect on anti-Dsg1 autoantibody pathogenicity in pemphigus foliaceus (PF) models.
source: they have an unexpected exacerbating effect on anti-Dsg1 autoantibody pathogenicity in pemphigus foliaceus (PF) models.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that PF24-9(IgG4) tends to be more pathogenic than PF24-9(IgG1) (Figure 4C) and that anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies are more pathogenic in FcγRα-null mice (Figure 4C).

claim: A non-pathogenic anti-Dsg1 antibody variant optimized for FcγR-mediated effector function can attenuate the skin lesions induced by pathogenic anti-Dsg1 antibodies.
source: Strikingly, a non-pathogenic anti-Dsg1 antibody variant optimized for FcγR-mediated effector function can attenuate the skin lesions induced by pathogenic anti-Dsg1 antibodies
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that non-pathogenic PF1-2-22(GASDALIE) reduced skin lesions induced by pathogenic PF1-8-15(N297A) (Figure 7B, C, D).

claim: FcγR-mediated effector function promotes the clearance of dead keratinocytes in PF models.
source: by promoting the clearance of dead keratinocytes.
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL staining data showing more apoptotic keratinocytes in mice treated with N297A variant compared to GASDALIE variant (Figure 6E, F).

claim: IgG effector function contributes to the clearance of autoantibody-Ag complexes, which is harmful in TTP.
source: These studies suggest that IgG effector function contributes to the clearance of autoantibody-Ag complexes, which is harmful in TTP
evidence: This is inferred from data showing that enhanced FcγR binding (GASDALIE variant) increases pathogenicity in TTP models (Figure 2H, I) and that FcγR deficiency reduces pathogenicity (Figure 2B, C, D, E).

claim: IgG effector function contributes to the clearance of autoantibody-Ag complexes, which is beneficial in PF.
source: but beneficial in PF and may provide new therapeutic opportunity.
evidence: This is inferred from data showing that enhanced FcγR binding (GASDALIE variant) reduces pathogenicity in PF models (Figure 5A-F) and that FcγR deficiency increases pathogenicity (Figure 4C).

claim: IgG4 has low affinity to FcγRs.
source: This is due to the unique features of IgG4, including its low affinity to FcγRs
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by binding data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C) and citations (Lighaam and Rispens, 2016; Vidarsson et al., 2014).

claim: IgG4 lacks capacity to activate complements.
source: and lack of capacity to activate complements
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations (Lighaam and Rispens, 2016; Vidarsson et al., 2014).

claim: IgG4 has reduced ability to form immune complex due to Fab-arm exchange.
source: as well as its reduced ability to form immune complex due to a unique process referred to as Fab-arm exchange (Lighaam and Rispens, 2016; Vidarsson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Fab-arm exchange between different IgG4 antibodies results in the formation of heterodimeric IgG4 molecules.
source: The Fab-arm exchange between different IgG4 antibodies results in the formation of heterodimeric IgG4 molecules (i.e., bi-specific IgG4 antibodies) that only allow monovalent binding (Koneczny, 2018; Lighaam and Rispens, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: The choice of IgG4 subclass in autoantibodies may be protective by reducing or preventing the pathogenic function of more harmful antibody classes or subclasses.
source: Given these features, it has been speculated that the choice of IgG4 subclass in autoantibodies in various relevant autoimmune diseases may be protective by reducing or preventing the pathogenic function of more harmful antibody classes or subclasses (Rihet et al., 1992).
evidence: This is presented as speculation from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: IgG4 autoantibodies targeting the acetylcholine receptor protect monkeys from myasthenia gravis induced by matched IgG1 autoantibodies.
source: IgG4 autoantibodies targeting the acetylcholine receptor have been reported to protect monkeys from myasthenia gravis induced by matched IgG1 autoantibodies (van der Neut Kolfschoten et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Allergen-specific IgG antibodies derived from hyperimmune beekeepers, mostly IgG4, are protective in allergy patients.
source: Allergen-specific IgG antibodies derived from hyperimmune beekeepers, mostly IgG4, have been reported to be protective in allergy patients (Devey et al., 1989) and mouse models (Schumacher et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Phospholipase A2-specific autoantibodies in patients with bee venom allergy switched from IgE to IgG4 after effective antigen-specific immunotherapy.
source: Phospholipase A2-specific autoantibodies in patients with bee venom allergy switched from IgE to IgG4 after effective antigen-specific immunotherapy (Akdis and Akdis, 2011; Devey et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: IgG4-mediated autoimmune diseases represent a unique category of more than 10 autoimmune conditions featured by the accumulation of pathogenic antigen-specific IgG4 autoantibodies.
source: IgG4-mediated autoimmune diseases represent a unique category of more than 10 autoimmune conditions featured by the accumulation of pathogenic antigen-specific IgG4 autoantibodies.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations (Huijbers et al., 2018; Koneczny, 2018).

claim: The pathogenic function of IgG4 autoantibodies has been either well established or highly suspected in the majority of IgG4-mediated diseases.
source: The pathogenic function of IgG4 autoantibodies has been either well established or highly suspected in the majority of these diseases (Huijbers et al., 2018; Koneczny, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: In PF, autoantibodies bind to Dsg1 (desmoglein 1), a desmoglein protein highly expressed in the superficial layers of the epidermis and essential for adhesion between neighboring keratinocytes.
source: In PF, autoantibodies bind to Dsg1 (desmoglein 1), a desmoglein protein highly expressed in the superficial layers of the epidermis and essential for adhesion between neighboring keratinocytes, and result in the loss of cell-cell adhesion and the blistering of skin (Anhalt et al., 1982; Korman et al., 1989; Rock et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies result in the loss of cell-cell adhesion and the blistering of skin in PF.
source: In PF, autoantibodies bind to Dsg1 (desmoglein 1), a desmoglein protein highly expressed in the superficial layers of the epidermis and essential for adhesion between neighboring keratinocytes, and result in the loss of cell-cell adhesion and the blistering of skin (Anhalt et al., 1982; Korman et al., 1989; Rock et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: ADAMTS13 is the critical enzyme maintaining the homeostasis of von Willebrand factor (vWF) in the plasma.
source: ADAMTS13 (a disintegrin and metalloproteinase with a thrombospondin type 1 motif, member 13), the critical enzyme maintaining the homeostasis of von Willebrand factor (vWF) in the plasma, is targeted by autoantibodies in acquired TTP (Zheng, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citation.

claim: ADAMTS13 is targeted by autoantibodies in acquired TTP.
source: ADAMTS13 (a disintegrin and metalloproteinase with a thrombospondin type 1 motif, member 13), the critical enzyme maintaining the homeostasis of von Willebrand factor (vWF) in the plasma, is targeted by autoantibodies in acquired TTP (Zheng, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citation.

claim: In both PF and TTP patients, IgG4 is a major autoantibody subclass.
source: In both PF and TTP patients, IgG4 is a major autoantibody subclass, and its levels correlate with disease activities (Ferrari et al., 2009; Rock et al., 1989; Sinkovits et al., 2018; Warren et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: IgG4 autoantibody levels correlate with disease activities in both PF and TTP patients.
source: In both PF and TTP patients, IgG4 is a major autoantibody subclass, and its levels correlate with disease activities (Ferrari et al., 2009; Rock et al., 1989; Sinkovits et al., 2018; Warren et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Polyclonal anti-Dsg1 and ADAMTS13 autoantibodies enriched from patient plasma are pathogenic in both in vitro assay and animal models.
source: Importantly, polyclonal anti-Dsg1 and ADAMTS13 autoantibodies enriched from patient plasma, as well as monoclonal anti-Dsg1 and -ADAMTS13 autoantibodies isolated from patients, are pathogenic in both in vitro assay and animal models (Huijbers et al., 2018; Koneczny, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Monoclonal anti-Dsg1 and -ADAMTS13 autoantibodies isolated from patients are pathogenic in both in vitro assay and animal models.
source: Importantly, polyclonal anti-Dsg1 and ADAMTS13 autoantibodies enriched from patient plasma, as well as monoclonal anti-Dsg1 and -ADAMTS13 autoantibodies isolated from patients, are pathogenic in both in vitro assay and animal models (Huijbers et al., 2018; Koneczny, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: IgG4 autoantibodies are pathogenic and highly relevant to the development of IgG4-mediated diseases.
source: These studies, together with the study of other IgG4-mediated diseases and IgG4-related diseases (Shiokawa et al., 2016), have established that IgG4 autoantibodies are pathogenic and highly relevant to the development of these diseases (Huijbers et al., 2018; Koneczny, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: IgG4 is the most prevalent IgG subclass in anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies and is associated with disease relapse.
source: Most studies supported the notion that IgG4 is the most prevalent IgG subclass in anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies and is associated with disease relapse (Ferrari et al., 2009; Sinkovits et al., 2018).

claim: IgG1 and IgG3 autoantibody levels appear to have a stronger correlation with disease severity in acquired TTP patients during the acute phase.
source: At the same time, IgG1 and IgG3 autoantibody levels appear to have a stronger correlation with disease severity in acquired TTP patients during the acute phase (Bettoni et al., 2012).

claim: Pathogenic anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies often have the IgG4 subclass in endemic PF patients.

evidence: This is stated as a summary of literature findings and supported by citations.

claim: Non-pathogenic anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies often have the IgG1 subclass in endemic PF patients.
source: In contrast, pathogenic anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies often have the IgG4 subclass, whereas non-pathogenic anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies often have the IgG1 subclass in endemic PF patients (Aoki et al., 2015; Warren et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of literature findings and supported by citations.

claim: Pathogenic and non-pathogenic anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies have different binding epitopes.
source: However, it is also reported that these pathogenic and non-pathogenic anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies have different binding epitopes (Aoki et al., 2015; Li et al., 2003).

claim: Some autoantibodies isolated from IgG4-mediated diseases (e.g., anti-Dsg1) are pathogenic in the form of scFv and Fab fragments.
source: Therefore, despite that IgG4 autoantibodies are pathogenic and that some autoantibodies isolated from IgG4-mediated diseases (e.g., anti-Dsg1) are pathogenic in the form of scFv and Fab fragments (Ishii et al., 2008; Rock et al., 1990; Yamagami et al., 2009)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Both humans and mice have activating and inhibitory FcγRs that mediate or inhibit antibody effector functions, respectively.
source: Both humans and mice have activating and inhibitory FcγRs that mediate or inhibit antibody effector functions, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Ablating activating FcγRs expression can protect autoimmune mice from premature mortality.
source: Either ablating activating FcγRs expression or ectopically overexpressing inhibitory FcγRIIB can protect autoimmune mice from premature mortality (Clynes et al., 1998a; McGaha et al., 2005)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Ectopically overexpressing inhibitory FcγRIIB can protect autoimmune mice from premature mortality.
source: Either ablating activating FcγRs expression or ectopically overexpressing inhibitory FcγRIIB can protect autoimmune mice from premature mortality (Clynes et al., 1998a; McGaha et al., 2005)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Ablating activating FcγRs expression or ectopically overexpressing inhibitory FcγRIIB can protect against arthritic antibody-induced joint inflammation in murine models.
source: as well as arthritic antibody-induced joint inflammation in murine models (Ji et al., 2002).

claim: Both murine and human IgG subclasses and Fc-FcγR interactions have a critical impact on the activities of blocking and agonistic antibodies.

claim: TTP1-420(IgG4) and TTP1-420(IgG1) have similar binding kinetics to human ADAMTS13.
source: These antibodies were confirmed to have similar binding kinetics to human ADAMTS13 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA binding data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both TTP1-420(IgG4) and TTP1-420(IgG1)-treated WT mice displayed a significant reduction in ADAMTS13 activity soon after the treatment.
source: As shown in Figure 1B, both TTP1-420(IgG4) and TTP1-420(IgG1)-treated WT mice displayed a significant reduction in ADAMTS13 activity soon after the treatment.
evidence: This is supported by ADAMTS13 activity assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The recovery of ADAMTS13 activity is significantly faster in TTP1-420(IgG4)-treated mice than in TTP1-420(IgG1)-treated mice.
source: However, the recovery of ADAMTS13 activity is significantly faster in TTP1-420(IgG4)-treated mice than in TTP1-420(IgG1)-treated mice, with almost complete recovery by day 8 in the former group and nearly no recovery in the latter group (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by ADAMTS13 activity assay data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: TTP1-420(IgG4) autoantibodies displayed weaker pathogenicity as compared to TTP1-420(IgG1) autoantibodies in FcγR-humanized mice.
source: Consistently, TTP1-420(IgG4) autoantibodies also displayed weaker pathogenicity as compared to TTP1-420(IgG1) autoantibodies in FcγR-humanized mice (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: This is supported by ADAMTS13 activity assay data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: While both IgG4 and IgG1 anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies can inhibit ADAMTS13 activity, IgG4 autoantibodies are less pathogenic as compared to IgG1 autoantibodies.
source: These results suggest that while both IgG4 and IgG1 anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies can inhibit ADAMTS13 activity, IgG4 autoantibodies are less pathogenic as compared to IgG1 autoantibodies.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing differential recovery rates of ADAMTS13 activity (Figure 1B, C, D, E).

claim: Switching to the IgG4 subclass in anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies represents a protective mechanism.
source: Therefore, it appears that switching to the IgG4 subclass in anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies represents a protective mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that IgG4 is less pathogenic than IgG1 in TTP models.

claim: Human IgG4 and IgG1 are very different in mediating FcγR-dependent effector function, with IgG4 being much less potent due to its weaker binding affinity to activating FcγRs.
source: Human IgG4 and IgG1 are very different in mediating FcγR-dependent effector function, with IgG4 being much less potent due to its weaker binding affinity to activating FcγRs (Bruhns et al., 2009; Vidarsson et al., 2014), including both mouse and human activating FcγRs (Bruhns et al., 2009; Derebe et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C, and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations and binding data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C).

claim: While TTP1-420(IgG1)-treated WT and FcγRα-null mice displayed comparable levels of reduction in ADAMTS13 activity at the early time points (day 1 and day 5), the recovery of ADAMTS13 activity is significantly faster in FcγRα-null mice.
source: As shown in Figure 2B, while TTP1-420(IgG1)-treated WT and FcγRα-null mice displayed comparable levels of reduction in ADAMTS13 activity at the early time points (day 1 and day 5) (Figure 2B), the recovery of ADAMTS13 activity is significantly faster in FcγRα-null mice (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: This is supported by ADAMTS13 activity assay data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: While FcγR-mediated function is not essential for the pathogenicity of anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies, it has an enhancing effect.
source: These results suggest that while FcγR-mediated function is not essential for the pathogenicity of anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies, it has an enhancing effect.
evidence: This is inferred from data showing that anti-ADAMTS13 antibodies can inhibit ADAMTS13 activity in FcγRα-null mice, but recovery is faster compared to WT mice (Figure 2B, C).

claim: Fcer1g-/- mice have accelerated recovery of ADAMTS13 enzyme activity compared to WT mice.
source: Further investigation in Fc receptor common γ-chain deficient mice (Fcer1g-/-), which lack functional activating FcγRs, showed that Fcer1g-/- mice have accelerated recovery of ADAMTS13 enzyme activity (Figure 2A, D, E)
evidence: This is supported by ADAMTS13 activity assay data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Activating Fcγ receptors are responsible for the enhancing effect of FcγRs to the pathogenicity of anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies.
source: suggesting that activating Fcγ receptors are responsible for the enhancing effect of FcγRs to the pathogenicity of anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies.
evidence: This is inferred from data showing that Fcer1g-/- mice (lacking activating FcγRs) have accelerated recovery of ADAMTS13 activity (Figure 2D, E).

claim: TTP1-420(N297A)-treated mice recovered much faster than TTP1-420(GASDALIE)-treated mice.
source: As shown in Figure 2F, while both TTP1-420(N297A) and TTP1-420(GASDALIE) autoantibodies induced a significant reduction in ADAMTS13 enzyme activity (Figure 2F), TTP1-420(N297A)-treated mice recovered much faster (Figure 2F, G).
evidence: This is supported by ADAMTS13 activity assay data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: The recovery of ADAMTS13 activity is faster in TTP1-420(IgG1)-treated mice than in TTP1-420(GASDALIE)-treated mice in hFCGR-Tg mice.
source: Consistently, both TTP1-420(IgG1) and TTP1-420(GASDALIE)-treated hFCGR-Tg mice induced a significant reduction in ADAMTS13 activity soon after the treatment (Figure 2H), and the recovery of ADAMTS13 activity is faster in TTP1-420(IgG1)-treated mice than in TTP1-420(GASDALIE)-treated mice (day 1 and day 5) (Figure 2H, I).
evidence: This is supported by ADAMTS13 activity assay data shown in Figure 2H and I.

claim: While the activating FcγR-mediated effector function is not absolutely required for the pathogenic function of anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies, it does have a critical enhancing effect, likely by depleting ADAMTS13-autoantibodies immune complex.
source: These results suggest that while the activating FcγR-mediated effector function is not absolutely required for the pathogenic function of anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies, it does have a critical enhancing effect, likely by depleting ADAMTS13-autoantibodies immune complex.
evidence: This is inferred from data showing that FcγR-enhanced variants (GASDALIE) have increased pathogenicity and slower recovery compared to FcγR-reduced variants (N297A) (Figure 2F, G, H, I).

claim: The majority of TTP samples analyzed were confirmed to contain anti-ADAMTS13 IgG autoantibodies, with 43 out of 44 TTP samples having anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibody signal levels that are twofold higher than healthy control average levels.
source: The majority of these samples were confirmed to contain anti-ADAMTS13 IgG autoantibodies, with 43 out of 44 TTP samples having anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibody signal levels that are twofold higher than healthy control (HC) average levels, which were considered as the background (Figure 3A, F).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3A and F.

claim: All TTP samples analyzed were confirmed to have severely reduced ADAMTS13 activity (with all samples having less than 5% ADAMTS13 activity).
source: All TTP samples were confirmed to have severely reduced ADAMTS13 activity (with all samples having less than 5% ADAMTS13 activity) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by ADAMTS13 activity assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: ADAMTS13 antigen levels were reduced in TTP patients.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Bettoni et al., 2012; Ferrari et al., 2009), ADAMTS13 antigen levels were also reduced (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3C and citations to previous reports.

claim: A correlation between ADAMTS13 activity and antigen levels was observed in TTP patients.
source: and a correlation between ADAMTS13 activity and antigen levels was observed (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Most TTP samples have both IgG1 and IgG4 autoantibodies.

claim: IgG1 and IgG4 anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies have an inverse correlation in TTP patients.
source: Further analysis of IgG1 and IgG4 anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies showed that most TTP samples have both IgG1 and IgG4 autoantibodies (Figure 3E, F) with an inverse correlation (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: IgG1 autoantibodies have a significant inverse correlation with ADAMTS13 antigen and activity levels in TTP patients.
source: Interestingly, while IgG1 autoantibodies have a significant inverse correlation with ADAMTS13 antigen and activity levels, IgG4 autoantibodies do not (Figure 3G-J)

claim: IgG4 autoantibodies do not have a significant inverse correlation with ADAMTS13 antigen and activity levels in TTP patients.
source: Interestingly, while IgG1 autoantibodies have a significant inverse correlation with ADAMTS13 antigen and activity levels, IgG4 autoantibodies do not (Figure 3G-J)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3I and J.

claim: IgG4 autoantibodies have relatively less impact on ADAMTS13 antigen and activity levels in TTP patients.
source: suggesting that IgG4 autoantibodies have relatively less impact on ADAMTS13 antigen and activity levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between IgG4 autoantibodies and ADAMTS13 antigen/activity levels (Figure 3I, J).

claim: While IgG1-dominant and IgG4-dominant TTP groups have similar ADAMTS13 activity levels, the IgG4-dominant group has significantly higher ADAMTS13 antigen levels.
source: Notably, while these two groups have similar ADAMTS13 activity levels (Figure 3L), the IgG4-dominant group has significantly higher ADAMTS13 antigen levels (Figure 3M).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3L and M.

claim: IgG4 anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies confer relatively less ADAMTS13 depletion.
source: These results suggest that IgG4 anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies confer relatively less ADAMTS13 depletion.
evidence: This is inferred from data showing that IgG4-dominant TTP samples have higher ADAMTS13 antigen levels despite similar activity levels compared to IgG1-dominant samples (Figure 3L, M).

claim: The IgG1 anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies are observed in both healthy subjects and endemic PF patients.

claim: The accumulation of IgG4 anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies is a key step in the development of PF disease.
source: Previously, it has been described that the IgG1 anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies are observed in both healthy subjects and endemic PF patients, and the accumulation of IgG4 anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies is a key step in the development of the disease (Warren et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of literature findings and supported by citation.

claim: The binding epitope of anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies is critical for the pathogenicity of anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies.
source: At the same time, the binding epitope of anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies is critical for the pathogenicity of anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies (Li et al., 2003)

claim: PF patients have both IgG4 and IgG1 anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies.

claim: IgG4 autoantibodies are much more abundant than IgG1 autoantibodies in PF patients.

claim: The IgG subclass of anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies could be a key variable in PF pathogenesis.
source: and that the IgG subclass of these anti-Dsg1 autoantibodies could be a key variable in PF pathogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from data showing that IgG1 and IgG4 autoantibodies have shared epitopes but different abundance (Figure 4A, B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Both human IgG4 and IgG1 anti-Dsg1 antibodies induced epidermal acantholysis in neonatal mice.
source: When tested in neonatal mice, both human IgG4 and IgG1 anti-Dsg1 antibodies induced epidermal acantholysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, C).

claim: The Fab fragment of anti-Dsg1 antibodies was sufficient to induce blisters in neonatal mice at comparable levels as intact IgG1 and IgG4 antibodies.

claim: Adult hFCGR-Tg mice treated with PF24-9(IgG1) autoantibodies could reproduce the clinical, histological, and immunological features of a skin lesion in PF patients.

evidence: This is supported by clinical, histological, and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Thickened epidermis and leukocyte infiltration were observed at the lesion sites during the disease onset in the adult PF mouse model.
source: In addition, we observed the thickened epidermis and leukocyte infiltration at the lesion sites during the disease onset, as well as crusting and scaling during the recovery (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, B)
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: Crusting and scaling were observed during the recovery in the adult PF mouse model.
